units.title: Sources
units.intro: In this unit you learn what history is, the kinds of sources, and how to tell primary sources from secondary sources.

pins.text: Oral tradition: stories told to the next generation

cards.title: Stories
body: People tell many stories. Many are **not true**.
They are **legends** or **fairy tales**.

cards.title: History is true
body: **History** is a true story.
It is about what **really happened**.

cards.title: The record of the past
body: History is the **record** of what happened in the past.
It tells us how people lived, their religion and their government.

cards.title: Change
body: History also tells us what changed.
It tells when, how and why it changed.

cards.title: Pre-history and history
body: Move the slider.

states.label: History
states.text: **History** began when people started **writing**, about **5000 years ago**.

cards.q: What is history?

options.B: A true story of what happened

cards.why: History is a true story about what really happened.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: History = the true record of the past.
Pre-history = before writing (more than 5000 years ago).

cards.title: How do we know?
body: History is based on **facts**.
To find facts we need **sources**.

cards.title: What is a source?
body: A source can be an old document.
It can also be a person who saw an event.

steps.text: **1. Oral tradition**: stories one generation tells the next generation.
**2. Archaeological remains**: coins, tools, weapons and buildings found under the ground.
**3. Written documents**: letters, diaries, books and inscriptions.
**4. Picture sources**: paintings, posters, photos, videos and films from that time.

cards.title: What is a generation?
body: You and your brothers and sisters are one **generation**.
Your parents are another. Your grandparents are another.

cards.title: Name the source
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: Evidence
body: All these sources give us **evidence**.
Evidence means **proof** of what happened.

cards.q: Coins and tools found under the ground are:
cards.why: Things found under the ground at historical places are archaeological remains.

cards.title: Memory trick: OAWP
body: "**O**ld **A**nswers **W**ait in **P**ictures."

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Sources: oral, archaeological, written, pictures.
Sources give evidence (proof).

cards.title: Can we trust it?
body: Sources must be **reliable**.
Reliable means we can depend on it.

cards.title: Written or oral?
body: Written stories are usually **more reliable** than oral stories.
Written stories do not change with time. Oral stories may change.

cards.title: Archaeological remains
body: They can be reliable. They show life at that time.
But sometimes we do not know their exact date.

cards.title: Primary or secondary?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Primary
states.text: A **primary source** comes from someone who **saw** the event. An eye-witness account, an interview or a diary.

states.label: Secondary
states.text: A **secondary source** comes **later**, from others. Stories passed on by mouth, and history textbooks.

cards.title: An eye-witness
body: You saw an accident. You can explain how it happened.
You are an **eye-witness**. Your account is probably correct.

cards.title: Stories change
body: A story passed from generation to generation may **change**.
So oral stories told later are secondary sources.

cards.title: Yohannes's diary
body: Yohannes went to Asmara Stadium. He wrote in his diary about the match.
Keih Bahri beat Asmara Birra 2–1.

cards.q: Yohannes wrote in his diary about the match he watched. His diary is:
cards.why: He saw the match himself and wrote it down. It is written and primary.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Primary = saw it. Secondary = heard or read it later.
Written sources are usually more reliable than oral ones.

units.title: Measuring Time
units.intro: In this unit you learn about dates, decades, centuries and millennia, time-lines and calendars.

cards.title: Units of time
body: We use **units of time** to say when things happened.
Hours, days and years are units of time.

cards.title: Clock and calendar
body: A **clock** measures hours and minutes.
A **calendar** shows days, weeks and months.

cards.title: History is past
body: All history happened in the **past**.

cards.title: A date
body: A **date** tells us **when** an event happened.
Eritrea was liberated on **24 May 1991**.

cards.title: Duration
body: **Duration** is **how long** something lasted.
Eritreans fought for liberation from **1961 to 1991**.

cards.title: How long was the struggle?
cards.problem: The armed struggle lasted from 1961 to 1991. How long was it?

steps.text: Take away the first year from the last year.

cards.q: "From 1961 to 1991" tells us the:
cards.why: It tells how long something lasted. That is duration.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Date = when. Duration = how long.

cards.title: Long periods
body: For long periods we use **decades**, **centuries** and **millennia**.
Millennia means more than one millennium.

cards.title: Bigger and bigger
body: Move the slider.

cards.title: Centuries in a millennium
cards.problem: How many centuries are in a millennium?

steps.text: A millennium is 1000 years. A century is 100 years.

cards.title: Remember: D-C-M
body: Each one is **10 times** bigger. Think "**D**ogs **C**hase **M**ice".

cards.title: Time-lines
body: A **time-line** is a line that shows time.
We mark the decades or centuries on it.

cards.title: Writing dates
body: Write the dates **below** or **above** the line.

cards.title: Read the family time-line
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Son
states.text: A son born in **1990**. That is **2 decades** after his mother.

cards.q: How many years are in a century?
cards.why: A century is a period of 100 years.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Decade 10, century 100, millennium 1000 years.
A time-line shows events in order.

cards.title: What is a calendar?
body: A **calendar** lists the days, weeks and months of the year.

cards.title: The Gregorian Calendar
body: The year we write today counts years since **Jesus Christ was born**.
This is the **Gregorian Calendar**. It began in **1582**.

cards.title: Who started it?
body: Pope Gregory started it in 1582.

cards.title: Three calendars
head: Calendar
Months
Note
rows: Counts from the birth of Christ
Used by the Orthodox Church in Eritrea

cards.title: A moon calendar
body: In Anno Hejira, a **new moon** means a **new month**.

cards.title: Chronology
body: The study of time is called **chronology**.

cards.title: A.D. and B.C.
body: **A.D.** means "in the year of the Lord". **B.C.** means **Before Christ**.
Write A.D. before the date. Write B.C. after it.

cards.title: C.E. and B.C.E.
body: Today we also say **C.E.** instead of A.D.
We say **B.C.E.** instead of B.C.

cards.title: Read the B.C.E. and C.E. line

steps.text: The middle is the **birth of Christ**.
**B.C.E.** years are on the left. They are **Before the Common Era**.
**C.E.** years are on the right. They are in the **Common Era**.

cards.title: Counting B.C.E. years
cards.problem: How many years from 3 B.C.E. to 1 B.C.E.?

steps.text: B.C.E. years count down towards Christ's birth.

cards.title: Counting C.E. years
cards.problem: How many years from C.E. 2 to C.E. 5?

steps.text: C.E. years count up.

cards.q: Which comes first on a time-line?
cards.why: B.C.E. years are before the Common Era, so they come first.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: B.C.E. = before. C.E. = after.
Gregorian: 12 months. Coptic: 13 months. Hejira: follows the moon.

cards.title: Eritrea colonised
body: Italy colonised Eritrea in **1890**.
Eritrea was liberated from Ethiopia in **1991**.

cards.title: About a century
body: The book says this lasted about **100 years**.
100 years is a **century**.

steps.text: C.E. 1 to C.E. 100 is the **1st century**.
C.E. 101 to C.E. 200 is the **2nd century**.
C.E. 201 to C.E. 300 is the **3rd century**.
C.E. 301 to C.E. 400 is the **4th century**.

cards.title: Our centuries
body: C.E. 1901 to 2000 is the **20th century**.
C.E. 2001 to 2100 is the **21st century**.

cards.title: Find the years of a century
cards.problem: The 9th century C.E. is from ___ to ___.

steps.text: The century ends at its number times 100.
It starts 99 years before that: 801.

cards.title: Centuries between dates
cards.problem: How many centuries from 300 B.C.E. to 100 B.C.E.?

cards.q: The 12th century C.E. is from:

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Century number × 100 = the last year.
The 20th century = 1901–2000.

units.title: Distance and Scale
units.intro: In this unit you learn what a map scale is, the three kinds of scales, how to change one into another, and how to find real distances.

pins.text: Scale: map distance and ground distance

cards.title: What is a map?
body: A **map** is a **flat picture** of the earth's surface.
It can show a region, a country or the whole world.

cards.title: Top view
body: A map shows the land **from the top**.

cards.title: What maps are for
body: Maps help us find **where** a place is.
They also help us find the **distance** between places.

cards.title: Maps choose
body: A map does **not** show everything.
It shows the things named in its **title**.

cards.title: Much smaller
body: A map is much **smaller** than the real area.
A short line on the map is a long way on the ground.

cards.title: Four parts of every map
body: Every map has a **title**, a **key**, a **compass rose** and a **scale**. Tap each dot.

cards.q: Which part of a map explains the symbols?
cards.why: The key tells you what each symbol means.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Map = flat picture of the earth from the top.
Title, key, compass rose, scale.

cards.title: Scale
body: The **scale** compares the distance **on the map** with the distance **on the ground**.
It tells how far apart places really are.

cards.title: A fraction
body: Scale = map distance ÷ ground distance.

cards.title: Find the scale
cards.problem: Town A to Town B is 500 km. On the map it is 5 cm. What is the scale?

steps.text: 5 cm on the map = 500 km on the ground.
So 1 cm on the map = 100 km.

cards.q: 5 cm on a map is 500 km on the ground. 1 cm is:

cards.title: Three kinds
body: We show a scale in **three** ways.
A scale statement, a representative fraction, or a graphic scale.

cards.title: See the three kinds
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Scale statement
states.text: A **scale statement** uses **words**. "1 cm to 1 km" means 1 cm on the map is 1 km on the ground.

states.label: Representative fraction
states.text: A **representative fraction** is a **ratio**, like 1 : 100,000. 1 cm is 100,000 cm.

states.label: Graphic scale
states.text: A **graphic scale** is a **short graph**. It is the **easiest** to use.

cards.title: Same units
body: In a representative fraction both numbers use the **same unit**.
1 cm is 100,000 cm. 1 inch is 100,000 inches.

cards.title: Good for everyone
body: So it works with **miles** or **kilometres**.
It does not matter which one a country uses.

steps.text: Put the edge of a **paper** between A and B.
Make a **dot** on the paper at A and at B.
Put the paper on the **graphic scale**. One dot is at 0.
Read the other dot. It is about **50 km**.

cards.title: Where is it?
body: The graphic scale is usually at the **bottom** of the map.

cards.title: Draw a graphic scale
body: Draw a line. Divide it into **equal parts**.
Split the left part into small parts for fractions of a kilometre.

cards.why: A ratio like 1 : 100,000 is a representative fraction.

cards.title: Remember: S-R-G
body: "**S**mall **R**uler **G**uides."

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Words = statement. Ratio = representative fraction. Graph = graphic scale.

steps.text: 1 cm on the map = 1,000,000 cm on the ground.

cards.problem: Change 1 cm to 7 km into a representative fraction.

cards.problem: Change 1 cm to 7 metres into a representative fraction.

steps.text: 1 metre = 100 cm.

cards.title: Straight line
body: With a scale, you can measure a distance in a **straight line**.

cards.title: Three steps
head: Step
What to do

Use the scale to find the ground distance.

cards.title: Map of 1 cm to 900 km
cards.problem: On a map, 1 cm is 900 km. A to B is 2 cm. How far is it?

steps.text: Each cm is 900 km.

cards.title: Class exercise
cards.problem: A to B is 5 cm. The scale is 1 cm to 90 km.

steps.text: Each cm is 90 km.

cards.problem: A to B is 3 cm. The scale is 1 : 7,000,000.

cards.title: Review question
cards.problem: The scale is 1 cm to 4 km. A to B is 5 cm.

steps.text: Each cm is 4 km.

cards.q: Scale 1 cm to 7 km. The map distance is 7 cm. The ground distance is:

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Ground distance = map distance × scale.

units.title: The Location and Size of Eritrea
units.intro: In this unit you learn where Eritrea is in Africa and the world, its neighbours, and how big it is.

pins.text: Eritrea, in the Horn of Africa

cards.title: Seven continents
body: The world has **seven continents**.
Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.

cards.title: Countries
body: Each continent has many **countries**.
But **Australia** is one country.

cards.title: Antarctica
body: **Antarctica** has no country.
People do not live there.

cards.title: Africa
body: The book says Africa has **53** independent countries.
Eritrea, Sudan, Egypt and Nigeria are some of them.

cards.title: Seven continents

letters.m: our continent, 53 countries in the book

body: Three start with **A-A-A**, plus North and South America, Antarctica and Europe.

cards.q: Which continent has no country?
cards.why: No people live in Antarctica, and it has no country.

cards.title: North of the Equator
body: Eritrea is **north of the Equator**.
So it is in the **Northern Hemisphere**.

cards.title: The Horn of Africa
body: Eritrea is in the **Horn of Africa**.
That is in **North East Africa**.

cards.title: By the sea
body: Eritrea is on the **western shore** of the **Red Sea**.

cards.title: Find Eritrea in Africa
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: Eritrea's neighbours
body: Tap each dot to see the neighbours.

cards.title: Lines on the globe
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Latitude
states.text: Eritrea is between about **12° N** and **18° N** latitude.

states.label: Longitude
states.text: Eritrea is between about **36° E** and **43° E** longitude.

cards.title: Latitude and longitude
body: **Latitude** is how far north or south of the Equator.
**Longitude** is how far east or west of the Prime Meridian.

cards.q: Which country borders Eritrea in the south?
cards.why: Ethiopia is to the south of Eritrea.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Eritrea: Northern Hemisphere, Horn of Africa, west shore of the Red Sea.
Neighbours: Sudan, Ethiopia, Djibouti; Yemen and Saudi Arabia across the sea.

cards.title: Area
body: Eritrea's area is **124,330 square kilometres**.

cards.title: Big and small neighbours
body: Eritrea borders **Sudan**, which the book calls the largest country.
It also borders **Djibouti**, one of the smallest in Africa.

cards.title: Eritrea in the world
body: The book says Eritrea is **96th** of 193 countries.
So it is larger than **97** countries.

cards.title: Smaller than Eritrea
body: Malawi, Benin, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Togo, Guinea Bissau and Lesotho are **smaller** than Eritrea.

cards.title: Over 360 islands
body: Eritrea has **over 360 islands**.
Together they are about **1335 km²**.

cards.title: Dahlak Kebir
body: The **largest** island is **Dahlak Kebir**. It is **643 km²**.
It is bigger than some countries, like Seychelles.

cards.title: Nora
body: **Nora** is the **second largest** island.

units.title: Migration
units.intro: In this unit you learn who came to Eritrea long ago, why people migrate, and how migration changes the environment.

cards.title: Migrants
body: People who move to live in another place are **migrants**.
Moving like this is called **migration**.

cards.title: The first people
body: The first people in Eritrea were the **pygmoid** people.
They were dark-skinned, stocky and short.

cards.title: The Nilotes
body: The **Nilotes** came from the **upper Nile**.
They mixed with the pygmoids.

cards.title: The Kushites
body: Around **2000 B.C.E.** the **Kushites** came from **north Africa**.
They were **pastoralists**. They moved with their herds.

cards.title: Kushite animals
body: They kept cows, oxen and goats.

cards.title: The Semites
body: Around **1000 B.C.E.** the **Semites** came from the **Arabian Peninsula**.
They settled in the **highlands**.

cards.title: What the Semites brought
body: They brought the **camel**, the **horse**, **sheep**, new plants and new ways of farming.
This led to **settled communities** and **government**.

cards.title: Semitic languages
body: The **Rashaida**, **Tigre** and **Tigrigna** speak Semitic languages.

steps.text: **Nilotes**: from the upper Nile.
**Kushites**: from north Africa, about 2000 B.C.E.
**Semites**: from Arabia, about 1000 B.C.E.
**Beja**: from the north, 7th–8th century C.E.
**Arabs**: to the Dahlak Islands and coast, 8th century.
**Assaimara Afar**: from the south-east, 16th–17th century.

cards.title: The Beja
body: In the **7th–8th century C.E.** the **Beja** came from the north.
They were Kushites. Their numbers grew, so they moved south.

cards.title: Belau and Bani Amir
body: The **Belau** came from the Beja. Many settled in Hirghigo, Hamasien, Akkele Guzai and Serae.
The **Bani Amir**, another Beja group, settled in **Gash Barka**.

cards.title: Islam arrives
body: In the **7th century**, the first **Muslims** came from Arabia.
In the 8th century Arabs settled on the **Dahlak Islands** and the coast.

cards.title: Islam spreads
body: This helped Islam spread along the coast and inland.

cards.title: Turks and Arabs
body: In the **16th century**, many Turks and Arabs settled on the coast.

cards.title: The Afar
body: The **Adaimara** Afar lived on the southern Red Sea coast.
The **Assaimara** Afar came from the south-east in the 16th–17th centuries. They joined together.

cards.title: Sahil
body: Semitic speakers and Beja people lived in the hills of **Sahil**.

cards.title: Asghede
body: **Asghede**, from the Tseneadegle clan, moved to Adi Nefas.
Then he and his followers went to the hills of Sahil.

cards.title: Tigre speakers
body: The early people of Sahil mixed with the newcomers.
They spoke the **Tigre** language.

cards.title: Eritrea's ethnic groups
body: The book's map shows **nine** groups. Tap each dot.

cards.q: Who came from the Arabian Peninsula around 1000 B.C.E.?
cards.why: The Semites came from Arabia around 1000 B.C.E.

cards.q: Who were the earliest people in Eritrea?
cards.why: The earliest inhabitants were the pygmoid people.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Pygmoids → Nilotes → Kushites (2000 B.C.E.) → Semites (1000 B.C.E.) → Beja, Arabs, Turks, Afar.
Today's people come from all these migrations.

cards.title: Why move?
body: People migrate for **different reasons**.

cards.title: A. To find land
body: Some farmers do not have **enough land**.
Or their land is **not fertile**. So they move to fertile land.

cards.title: B. To find work
body: People with no work move to find **jobs**.
Some move for **higher wages**.

cards.title: Going far
body: Many Eritreans have gone to **Europe** or **North America** to work.

cards.title: C. Freedom
body: Some people move for **political** or **religious freedom**.
They want to escape their government.

cards.title: Choice or not?
body: Some people **choose** to migrate.
Others are **forced** to move.

cards.q: A farmer's land is not fertile. He moves to find:
cards.why: Shortage of land or poor land makes farmers move to fertile land.

cards.title: Why people move: L-W-F
body: "**L**et's **W**alk **F**ar."

cards.title: Cutting trees
body: Farmers cut down trees to make fields.
This is **deforestation**.

cards.title: Deforestation leads to…
head: Problem
Meaning
rows: Soil is washed or blown away
No rain for a long time

cards.title: Asmara grows
body: Many people come to **Asmara** from the countryside and abroad.

cards.title: Why Asmara?
body: Asmara is the **capital**. Almost all industries are there.
It has schools, hospitals, shops and **jobs**.

cards.title: Returnees
body: Many people who came back from Ethiopia settled in Asmara.

cards.q: Which problem comes from deforestation?
cards.why: Deforestation leads to erosion, less ground water, extinction and drought.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Migration → cutting trees → erosion, drought.
Big cities → pollution, traffic, shortages.

similar.a: To find work or higher wages.

questions.answer: It is the capital, with industries, services and jobs.

units.title: Settlement
units.intro: In this unit you learn what a settlement is, where people choose to build, the types and shapes of settlements, and how villages differ from towns.

pins.text: Hill: easy to defend from enemies
Roads meet: easy to reach other places

cards.title: To settle
body: To **settle** means to stay or live in a place.
A **settlement** is a place where people live.

cards.title: Big or small
body: A settlement can be **one house** or many buildings.
It can be **permanent** or **temporary**.

cards.title: Buildings
body: A big settlement has homes, schools, shops, offices, factories, churches and mosques.

cards.title: Why build houses?
body: After **food**, a house is the most important human need.

cards.title: Hamlets to cities
body: People group into **hamlets**, **villages**, **towns** and **cities**.
Settlements are **rural** or **urban**.

cards.q: After food, what is the most important need?
cards.why: The book says after food, a house (settlement) is the most important need.

cards.title: Location
body: The **location** of a settlement is the place where it is built.

cards.title: Why here?
body: Our ancestors chose places for good reasons. Tap each dot.

cards.title: Safe from floods
body: People also chose land that was **safe from floods**.

cards.title: Fertile soil
body: Some farm areas have too many people and too little land.
Farmers move to **fertile** land and start a new settlement.

cards.title: Forests
body: **Lumbering** means cutting trees for **timber**.
Timber makes furniture and houses. Workers need homes, so a settlement grows.

cards.title: Minerals
body: Deserts often have no people.
But **minerals**, like oil and gas in Arabia, can bring settlement.

cards.title: Fish
body: The Southern Red Sea is hot and dry. Few people live inland.
Many live on the **coast** because of **fish**, in Thio, Ingel and Eddi.

cards.title: Today's reasons: F-F-M-F
body: Three **F**s and one **M**.

cards.q: Why do many people live on the coast of the Southern Red Sea?
cards.why: Plenty of fish attracts people to the coast.

cards.title: Four ways to group
body: We sort settlements by type: **dispersed** or **nucleated**.
Also by **shape**, and as **rural** or **urban**.

cards.title: Spread out or close together?
body: Move the slider.

cards.title: Cold and dry areas
body: Very cold areas are too cold for crops. Dry areas have too little rain.
People keep animals, so houses are far apart.

cards.title: Rocky and hilly areas
body: Farming is hard on rocks and hills.
So settlement is **dispersed**.

cards.title: Not enough resources
body: Some areas lack water or good soil.
People live apart to get enough.

cards.title: Why nucleated?
body: Enough **water** and **fertile soil** support many people.

cards.title: Defence and roads
body: People live together for **defence**.
Many towns grow where **roads meet**.

cards.q: In rocky and hilly areas, settlement is usually:
cards.why: Farming is difficult there, so houses are scattered.

cards.title: Three shapes
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Square
states.text: **Square** or **compact**: houses close together, spread equally in all directions.

states.label: Star
states.text: **Star-shaped**: houses go out in several directions, along rivers or roads.

states.label: Linear
states.text: **Linear**: houses in lines along a **road**, **river** or **coast**.

cards.title: Look around
body: Is your village compact, star-shaped or linear?

cards.q: Houses in a line along a road form a:
cards.why: Houses along roads, rivers or coasts make a linear settlement.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Compact = a square. Star = arms out. Linear = a line.

cards.title: Village or town?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Rural
states.text: **Rural**: villages. Most people **farm**. Houses are far apart.

states.label: Urban
states.text: **Urban**: towns. People work in trade, factories and offices. Houses are crowded.

cards.title: Land use in towns
body: Towns mix homes, industries, services and open public places.

cards.title: Environment matters
body: In dry areas people keep animals.
So they build houses far apart, with land for the animals.

cards.title: Words for work
body: **Mining** is digging minerals from the earth.
**Quarrying** is digging out stones and sand for building.

cards.q: In rural areas, most people work in:
cards.why: In rural settlements most of the workforce is in farming.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Rural = farming, few services, spaced houses.
Urban = many jobs and services, crowded houses.

questions.q: If a settlement follows the direction of a road, it is ___.

why: A settlement means a place where people live.

units.title: Culture and Beliefs
units.intro: In this unit you learn about the nine ethnic groups of Eritrea, our music, art and crafts, and our holidays.

pins.text: Tigre: lowlands, from Sudan to the coast
Bidhaawyeet: between western Barka and Sahel
Saho: south of Asmara and Massawa
Rashaida: coast of Semhar and Sahel
Afar tent: half-circle, hides and mats
Tent (ablo, agnet): nomads can move it

cards.title: Nine groups
body: Eritrea has **nine ethnic groups**.
They mix together, but most live in their **traditional areas**.

cards.title: Where do they live?
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: Afar: where and work
body: The **Afar** live on the south-east coast (Southern Red Sea) and on the islands.
Most are **herders**. Some trade or fish.

cards.title: Afar: food and home
body: They eat milk, fish and meat.
Nomadic Afar live in **half-circle tents** of hides and mats. Camels carry them.

cards.title: Afar: faith
body: In a few **oases** they grow maize and tobacco.
The Afar are **Muslims** and speak **Afar**.

cards.title: Bilen
body: The **Bilen** live in and around **Keren** (Anseba).
Some are **Christian** and some **Muslim**.

cards.title: Bilen: life
body: Many farm; others are herders. They speak **Bilen**.
Huts are common in the countryside.

cards.title: Bidhaawyeet
body: The **Bidhaawyeet** live between western **Barka** and **Sahel**.
They come from the **Beja**.

cards.title: Bidhaawyeet: life
body: Most are **semi-nomadic** herders of camels, goats and sheep.
They travel far to find **pasture**.

cards.title: Bidhaawyeet: food
body: They eat flat bread and boiled or roasted cereals.
At feasts they eat grilled meat called **mada**.

cards.title: Bidhaawyeet: home
body: They live in tents called **himar** (agnet), which are easy to move.
They are **Muslim** and speak Bidhaawyeet.

cards.title: Kunama
body: The **Kunama** live in Gash Barka, around **Barentu**.
Some are Christian, some Muslim. A few believe in the creator **Anna**.

cards.title: Kunama: life
body: Most farm. They also keep cattle, goats and sheep.
They eat **tukusa**, a thick porridge of sorghum or millet.

cards.title: Nara
body: The **Nara** live on the western slopes and the **Barka plains**.
They are mainly **farmers**. They also keep animals.

cards.title: Nara: life
body: They eat vegetables and traditional bread.
They live in huts in villages and speak **Nara**.

cards.title: Rashaida
body: The **Rashaida** came from **Arabia** in the 19th century.
They are **nomads** who live in tents.

cards.title: Rashaida: life
body: They keep goats and camels, and trade.
They live on the coast of Semhar and Sahel. They are Muslim and speak **Arabic**.

cards.title: Saho
body: The **Saho** live south of Asmara and Massawa, and in the highlands.
Most are **Muslim**.

cards.title: Saho: life
body: Many Saho are now **settled farmers**. Some keep **bees**.
They live in groups with a common ancestor and speak **Saho**.

cards.title: Tigre
body: The **Tigre** live in the **lowlands**, from Sudan to the coast.
Most are seasonal farmers and herders.

cards.title: Tigre: moving
body: After the rains they move with their herds to Samhar, Sahil and northern Barka.

cards.title: Tigre: food and faith
body: They eat cereals and hard porridge called **akalet**.
Most are Muslim; some are Christian. They speak **Tigre**.

cards.title: Tigrigna
body: Most **Tigrigna** are settled farmers in the crowded **central highlands**.
Most are **Orthodox Christians**. A few Muslims are called **Jeberti**.

cards.title: Tigrigna crops
body: They grow barley, wheat, taff, dagusha, flax, potatoes, peas and beans.

cards.title: Kinds of houses
body: People build houses to suit their way of life. Tap each dot.

cards.title: The nine groups at a glance
head: Group
Main work
Religion

cards.title: Highlands and lowlands
body: Highland people are mostly **settled farmers**.
Lowland people mostly **herd** animals.

cards.title: Different but alike
body: Each group is special. But they have **many things in common**.

cards.q: Tukusa is a porridge eaten by the:
cards.why: Tukusa is a common Kunama food.

cards.q: Which group came from Arabia in the 19th century?
cards.why: The Rashaida came from the Hijaz (Arabia) in the 19th century.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Nine groups, each with its own area.
Highlands = farmers. Lowlands = herders.

cards.title: Music and dance
body: Every group has its own **music** and **dances**.
People make their own instruments.

cards.title: Instruments
body: These are the Tigrigna names. Tap each dot.

cards.title: Many names
body: Other groups have these too, except the wata.
The kirar is **kira-abangala** (Kunama), **masanko** (Nara), **massankoob** (Bidhaawyeet).

cards.title: When we play
body: Music is played at **ceremonies**, like births, marriages and feasts.

cards.title: Oral traditions
body: All groups have poems, proverbs, songs, chants, folk tales, legends and histories.

cards.title: Plays
body: Traditional drama uses music, dancing and acting.
During the liberation struggle, people wrote **new plays**.

cards.title: Paintings
body: Old paintings were done on **skin** or **canvas**.
Most church walls have colourful paintings.

cards.title: Pottery
body: Eritreans have made **pots** since ancient times.
Coffee-pots, cups, clay pots, water pots and incense holders.

cards.title: Jewellery
body: Each group has its own jewellery.
Men give gold and silver earrings, necklaces and rings to brides.

cards.title: Leather and baskets
body: **Leather work** and **basketry** are common.
Leather is decorated with **beads** and **shells**.

cards.title: Wood-carving
body: Many carvings are made from **olive wood**.

cards.q: The kebero is a:
cards.why: Kebero means drum.

cards.title: Instruments: K-W-S-K
body: "**K**ids **W**ho **S**ing **K**indly."

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Culture: music, dance, oral tradition, drama, painting, crafts.

cards.title: National days
body: Move the slider.

cards.title: Religious holidays
body: Id Al Fitir, Id Al Adha, Timqet, Christmas, Easter and Meskel are holidays too.
People pray and hold feasts.

cards.title: Meskel
body: At **Meskel**, Christians remember the finding of the True Cross.
They light a **bonfire** called **Damera**.

cards.title: How we celebrate
body: Independence Day has parades, songs and dances.
On Martyrs' Day people hold **candle-light marches**.

cards.title: Eritrea Festival
body: At the **Annual Eritrea Festival**, all groups show songs, dances and plays.
Houses, food, crops, instruments and crafts are shown too.

cards.q: Independence Day is on:
cards.why: Independence Day is 24 May.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: 24 May Independence. 20 June Martyrs. 1 Sept Armed Struggle.

units.title: Eritrea 900 B.C.E.–1300 C.E.
units.intro: In this unit you learn how people lived in ancient Eritrea, the Red Sea trade, the Beja kingdoms and the coming of Islam.

cards.title: Farming
body: Since early times, **farming** was important.
People also raised farm animals.

cards.title: Crafts
body: By the **first century C.E.** people had **crafts**.
Metalwork, pottery, carving and building.

cards.title: The Red Sea trade
body: The Red Sea was a trade route between **Europe**, **Asia** and **Africa**.
So coastal Eritrea was important for trade.

cards.title: Merchants
body: Merchants from **Egypt** and **Greece** came to the Eritrean coast.

cards.title: The Land of Punt
body: The southern Red Sea coast was called the **Land of Punt**.
Coastal Eritrea was part of it.

cards.title: Queen Hatshepsut
body: In **1500 B.C.**, **Queen Hatshepsut** of Egypt sent ships to Punt for goods.

cards.title: Trading towns
body: Trade made towns grow from the coast to the interior.
Adulis, Kohaito, Keskesse, Matara, Toconda and Arato.

cards.title: Find the ancient towns
body: Tap each dot.

steps.text: Ships bring goods across the **Red Sea**.
Goods arrive at the port of **Adulis**.
Goods go to markets in **Kohaito**, **Matara** and **Toconda**.
Then they reach the **interior**.
Goods going out use the **same route** back.

cards.title: City-states
body: Adulis, Kohaito, Matara, Toconda and Keskesse were like **city-states**.
Each had **its own government**.

cards.title: Many gods
body: Long ago people believed in **many gods**.
The Semites added South Arabian gods: sun, moon, Venus and earth.

cards.title: Greek gods
body: From the **3rd century**, Greek gods came.
**Zeus** (father of gods), **Ares** (war) and **Poseidon** (sea).

cards.title: Christianity
body: **Christianity** came in the **middle of the 4th century**.
It was brought by **Frumentius** and **Aedesius**, from Syria.

cards.title: Writing
body: The Semites brought the **Sabean alphabet**.
There is a Sabean inscription at **Matara**.

cards.title: Greek language
body: Leaders used a little **Greek**. At first the Church used it too.
By the 4th century, Greek was used less.

cards.title: Geez
body: In the **5th century** the Bible was put into **Geez**.
Geez replaced Greek as the **official language**.

cards.title: The Periplus
body: The **Periplus of the Eritrean Sea** is a 1st century book.
Its writer visited the region and saw the trade.

cards.title: Coloe

units.title: The Period of the Bahri Negestat
units.intro: In this unit you learn about the Bahri Negestat, the Turks on the coast, the Portuguese and the Gragn wars, and why the Bahri Negestat grew weak.

The highlands: ruled by the Bahri Negestat

cards.title: Land by the Sea
body: **Midri Bahri** means "**Land by the Sea**".
Its ruler was the **Bahri Negassi**, "**Lord of the Sea**".

cards.title: Bigger rule
body: Early communities had **local rule** but were separate.
The Bahri Negestat ruled **larger areas**.

cards.title: At the top
body: At their strongest they ruled **most of the highlands**.
Early on, they also ruled the **coast**.

cards.title: When?
body: The first rulers with this title came in the **1300s**.
By the **1400s** they were quite powerful.

cards.title: Many rulers
body: From the 15th to 18th centuries there were many Bahri Negestat.
They were **not from one family**.

cards.title: Local chiefs
body: A Bahri Negassi was a strong local ruler.
He had **authority over local chiefs**.

cards.title: Abyssinia
body: Local people accepted them.
But **Abyssinian kings** tried to control them.

cards.title: Their lands
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: Debarwa
body: The capital was at **Debarwa**.
It was on the **trade route** of the 14th and 15th centuries.

cards.title: Council of Elders

cards.title: A new danger
body: From the 16th century, the **Turks** on the coast were a **threat**.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Bahri Negassi = Lord of the Sea. Capital = Debarwa.

cards.title: The Ottoman Empire
body: In the early 16th century the **Turkish (Ottoman) Empire** took Egypt, Sudan and most of Arabia.
Then Turkish ships came to Eritrea.

cards.title: Turks on the coast
body: The Turks first landed on the coast in **1517**.
By **1557** they controlled **Massawa** and **Hirghigo**.

cards.title: Massawa
body: Massawa was a **big port**.
Ships brought goods and took goods from the highlands.

cards.title: Pay the tax
body: Anyone trading at Massawa paid a **tax** to the Turks.
The Turks **could not** control the highlands.

cards.title: The Naib
body: The Turks ruled the coast through the **Naib**.
He was head of the **Belau** family and the Turks' **deputy**.

steps.text: Traders at the port pay **tax**.
The **Naib** collects it.
He gives a share to the **Turks**.
He gives a share to the **Bahri Negestat**.

cards.title: Friendly orders
body: Rulers in **Istanbul** told the Naibs to be friendly with the Bahri Negestat.

cards.title: Naib as judge
body: The Naibs had a lot of power over **Samhar**.
They judged quarrels and decided who owned the grazing lands.

cards.q: The Naib was:

cards.why: The Naib was head of the Belau family and the Turks' deputy.

lessons.title: The Portuguese, the Turks and Gragn

cards.title: The Portuguese
body: In the 16th century, **Portuguese** priests and traders came.
They wanted to **trade with India**.

cards.title: Their plan
body: They wanted to control the trade routes to the East.
So they tried to be friends with the **king of Abyssinia** to beat the Turks.

cards.title: Gragn
body: **Gragn** was a Muslim leader in Abyssinia.
He fought the Abyssinian king. The **Turks helped** him.

cards.title: Two sides
body: The Abyssinian king asked the **Portuguese** for help.
He sent **Bahri Negassi Yeshaq** to attack the Turks.

cards.title: The result
body: Gragn was **defeated**. Yeshaq took **Massawa** from the Turks.
But in **1560** the Turks came back and took Massawa again.

cards.title: After the wars
body: The Bahri Negestat often disagreed with the Abyssinian kings.
There was much fighting between them.

cards.q: Who helped Gragn?
cards.why: Gragn was helped by the Turks.

units.title: Natural Resources and Conservation
units.intro: In this unit you learn what resources are, renewable and non-renewable resources, and how to conserve soil, water, forests, grazing land, wildlife and minerals.

pins.text: Grass: food for goats, sheep, cattle
Latrine built far from the water
Animals have their own watering place
Trees help rain soak into the ground

cards.title: What is a resource?
body: A **resource** is anything **useful** to people.
Rocks, plants, animals, soil, water and chalk are resources.

cards.title: Natural resources
body: **Natural resources** come directly from **nature**.
People use them to make useful things.

cards.title: Resources from nature
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: Soil
body: Plants need **soil** to grow. Soil gives them water and minerals.
Plants give us food and **oxygen**. There is **no life without soil**.

cards.title: Grass
body: Goats, sheep and cattle eat **grass**.
They give us milk, butter, cheese, skin and wool.

cards.title: The atmosphere
body: The **atmosphere** is the air around the earth.
It has **oxygen**. Our bodies use it to change food into **energy**.

cards.title: Rain and protection
body: Clouds form from water vapour, and bring rain.
The atmosphere also stops harmful rays from the sun.

cards.title: The Red Sea
body: The **Red Sea** is rich in **fish**, **salt** and other minerals.

cards.title: Trees
body: Trees give **timber** and **medicine**.
Also rubber, palm oil, coffee, spices and chewing gum.

cards.title: Stone
body: **Stone** is used to build houses.

cards.q: Why is there no life without soil?

options.B: Plants grow in soil and give food and oxygen

cards.why: Plants need soil; we need plants for food and oxygen.

cards.title: Two groups
body: Natural resources are **renewable** or **non-renewable**.

cards.title: Renewable
body: **Renewable** resources can be used **again and again**.
Water, oxygen, soil, plants, animals, fish, wind, waves and tides.

cards.title: They replace themselves
body: Plants and animals **reproduce**, so they replace themselves.

cards.title: Keeping the air balanced
body: In the day, plants take in **carbon dioxide** and give out **oxygen**.
Animals always breathe in oxygen. So the air stays **balanced**.

cards.title: Energy from nature
body: The **sun** gives solar power. We can store it in a **battery**.
We can also get power from **water**.

cards.title: Use them well
body: Nature cannot renew resources if we use them **wrongly**.
If we cut trees, we must **plant new ones**.

cards.title: Keep soil fertile
body: Crops take minerals from the soil.
Farmers add **manure** to put them back.

cards.title: Crop rotation
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Year 3
states.text: Year 3: the first crop can come back.

cards.title: Non-renewable
body: **Non-renewable** resources are found in **fixed amounts**.
They **cannot replace themselves**.

cards.title: Minerals
body: Iron, silver, aluminium, coal, gas, gold, copper, sulphur, potash and salt are non-renewable.
Once used up, they never come back.

cards.title: More people
body: More people need more cars, houses and factories.
So we must use minerals **carefully**.

cards.q: Which is non-renewable?
cards.why: Iron is found in a fixed amount and cannot replace itself.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Renewable = can renew (plants, water, soil).
Non-renewable = fixed amount (minerals, oil, gas).

cards.title: What is conservation?
body: **Conservation** is the careful use and protection of natural resources.

cards.title: Stop the waste
head: Step
Example
rows: Metal containers, cars, tyres, bottles, newspaper

cards.title: Soil takes time
body: Soil takes **thousands of years** to form.
Careless people can destroy it in a few years.

cards.title: Erosion
body: Rain and wind can carry away the top soil.
Plants protect soil. Cutting them makes erosion worse.

cards.title: Saving soil on slopes
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Bare slope
states.text: On a bare slope, rain washes soil **down**.

states.label: Contour ploughing
states.text: **Contour ploughing**: plough **across** the slope. Ridges hold the water.

states.label: Terracing
states.text: **Terracing**: make **steps** on the hill. The flat ground slows erosion.

cards.title: Trees and bushes
body: Plant trees. Leave natural plants between fields.

cards.title: Mulching
body: **Mulching** is covering soil with old grass, stalks and leaves.
It keeps water in and weeds down.

cards.title: More ways to keep soil fertile
body: Use crop rotation, **green manure** and **mulching**.
Leave a field **fallow** (no crops) some years.

cards.title: Water for everyone
body: We need clean water to drink, wash, cook and farm.
Dry places must **save** water and keep it clean.

cards.title: Dams
body: **Dams** store rainwater for the whole year.
We can even raise fish in them.

cards.title: Keep water clean
body: Tap each dot to see how to protect water.

cards.title: No chemicals
body: Do not put harmful chemicals in water.
Remove rubbish, dead leaves and sticks.

cards.title: Why forests?
body: Forests give timber, firewood, food and medicine.
They are **homes for wildlife** and save water and soil.

cards.title: Protecting forests
head: Best ways to protect forests
rows: Keep grazing land separate from crop land.
Don't put too many animals on one area.
Protect forests for wildlife to breed.
Reafforest: replant where forests were cut.
Afforest: plant trees where there were none.

cards.title: Grazing lands
body: Grazing lands are dry lands covered with grass.
**Overgrazing** kills the grass. Weeds grow instead.

cards.title: Stop overgrazing
body: Don't put **too many animals** on the land.
Use **rotational grazing** so grass grows back.

cards.title: Wildlife in danger
body: Hunting and destroying habitats can make animals **extinct**.

cards.title: Saving wildlife
body: The government can **forbid hunting** by law.
It can make **national parks**.

cards.title: Minerals
body: Waste less when processing minerals.
**Re-use** metals: old cars, cans and glass.

cards.title: Substitutes
body: Plastic can replace some metal things.
**Solar**, **wind** and **geothermal** energy can replace oil, gas and coal.

units.title: Economic Activities
units.intro: In this unit you learn why different work happens in different places, and the three kinds of economic activity.

cards.title: Two environments
body: Work depends on the **natural** and the **cultural** environment.

cards.title: Physical environment
body: The **physical environment** is soil, climate, plants, water, landforms and other resources.
Farmers grow crops to suit the climate and soil.

cards.title: Hot crops
body: Cotton, palm oil, cocoa, groundnuts, coffee and bananas need **high temperature**.
They grow in **tropical** zones.

cards.title: Highlands and lowlands
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Highlands
states.text: **Wheat** and **barley** need **low** temperature. They grow in Eritrea's highlands.

states.label: Lowlands
states.text: **Sorghum** and **sesame** need **high** temperature. They grow in Eritrea's lowlands.

cards.title: Soil and crops
body: Different crops need different minerals.
Wheat and maize need **nitrates**. Potatoes need **potash**.

cards.title: Poor soil
body: Soils poor in minerals are left for **grazing** animals.

cards.title: Forests and fish
body: In rich forests, **lumbering** is the main work.
On the coast of Eritrea, **fishing** is the main work.

cards.title: Latitude
body: Climate changes from the Equator to the Poles.
So different crops grow at different latitudes.

cards.title: Food we like
body: The food people **prefer** usually grows nearby.

cards.title: Favourite foods
head: Place
Preferred food
rows: N. America, Australia, Argentina, Russia, Ukraine

cards.q: Which crop grows in Eritrea's hot lowlands?
cards.why: Sorghum and sesame need high temperature, so they grow in the lowlands.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Climate and soil decide crops.
People prefer the food that grows near them.

cards.title: Three kinds
body: Economic activities are **primary**, **secondary** and **tertiary**.

steps.text: **Primary**: get things **directly from nature**. A farmer grows wheat.
**Secondary**: **change** primary products into new things. Wheat becomes bread.
**Tertiary**: **services** and trade. A shop sells the bread.

cards.title: Early people
body: Early people hunted, gathered fruit and fished.
Later came farming, grazing, forestry, mining and quarrying.

cards.title: Primary industry
body: In primary work you use resources **as they are**.
They come straight from nature.

cards.title: Primary activities
body: Each person gets something straight from nature. Tap each dot.

cards.title: Secondary: handcrafts
body: **Handcrafts**: pottery, weaving, mats, woodwork and metal work.
They make pots, clothes, axes, baskets, ploughs and more.

cards.title: Before modern industry
body: Handcrafts were the main industry in Eritrea before the Italian period.

cards.title: Secondary: modern industry
body: Building, steel, ships, furniture, cars, textiles and chemicals.
Modern industry started in Eritrea during the **Italian administration**.

cards.title: Tertiary: traders
body: **Traders** buy crops, fish and salt and sell them in towns.
They also sell factory goods to farmers and fishermen.

cards.title: Tertiary: services
body: Buses sell **transport**. Hotels sell rooms and food.
Pharmacies, shops and banks are tertiary too.

cards.q: A bakery that makes bread from flour is:
cards.why: It changes a primary product into something new.

cards.q: A bus that carries people for money is:
cards.why: Transport is a service, so it is tertiary.

cards.title: P-S-T

cards.title: Remember this!

why: Primary activities get resources directly from the natural environment.

similar.q: Is getting salt from sea-water primary?

questions.q: What is a secondary activity? Give an example.
questions.answer: Changing primary products into other things, e.g. pottery or making furniture.
why: Secondary activities process the products of primary activity.

similar.q: When did modern industry start in Eritrea?

questions.q: What is a tertiary activity? Give an example.
questions.answer: Services and business, e.g. shops, transport, hotels or banks.
why: Tertiary activities provide services.

questions.q: Soil and climate are parts of the cultural environment.
why: They are parts of the physical environment.

similar.q: Name part of the physical environment.
similar.a: Soil, climate, vegetation, water or landforms.

questions.q: Wheat and barley are dominant in hot climates.
why: Wheat and barley need low temperature (highlands).

similar.q: Which crops need high temperature in Eritrea?

questions.q: Handcraft is a good example of tertiary activity.
why: Handcraft changes raw materials into goods, so it is secondary.

questions.q: Food habits of people can influence the distribution of crops.
why: People prefer and grow the food of their area.

questions.q: Why is the coast of Eritrea good for fishing?
why: Coastal areas rich in fish make fishing the main activity.

similar.q: Where is lumbering the main activity?

questions.q: In most countries of Asia and the Middle East people prefer:
why: The book says people there prefer rice.

similar.q: What do most African countries prefer?

questions.q: Why do different crops grow in different areas?
questions.answer: Because of differences in climate (temperature) and soil minerals.
why: Crops need different temperatures and different minerals.

similar.q: What else affects the location of economic activities?

questions.q: Which was the main industry in Eritrea before modern industry?
why: Handicraft was the main type of industry before the Italian period.

units.title: Disaster
units.intro: In this unit you learn what disasters are, and the causes, effects and solutions for floods, droughts and lightning.

cards.title: Disaster
body: A **disaster** causes a lot of **damage** and puts people in **danger**.

cards.title: Natural disasters
body: A **natural disaster** is caused by nature.
Earthquakes, volcanoes, lightning, storms, tides and floods.

cards.title: Human-made disasters
body: People can cause disasters too.
Floods, drought, deforestation, erosion and pollution.

cards.title: Famine
body: Floods and droughts destroy our **food**.
This can cause **famine** (people have no food).

cards.q: Which is a natural disaster?
cards.why: Earthquakes are caused by nature.

cards.title: What is a flood?
body: A **flood** happens when a river has **too much water**.
The water **overflows** its banks.

cards.title: Damage
body: Floods destroy farms and houses.
They kill animals and people.

cards.title: Watch a river flood
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Normal
states.text: Normal: the river stays in its **channel**.

states.label: Heavy rain
states.text: **Heavy rain** for hours or days. The ground gets **soaked**.

states.label: Flood
states.text: The water runs over the surface. The river **overflows**!

states.label: Shallow river
states.text: Soil in the river makes it **shallow**. It floods more easily.

cards.title: Natural cause
body: **Heavy rain** is the natural cause.
Soaked (**saturated**) ground cannot take in more water.

steps.text: People **cut down trees**. Roots no longer hold the soil.
Rain **washes soil** down the mountains.
Soil settles in the river. The river bed **rises**.
The shallow river **overflows** and destroys crops.

cards.title: Towns and floods
body: Towns cover the ground with **tar**, **cement** and buildings.
Rain cannot soak in, so it runs into rivers.

cards.title: Control: plant trees
body: **Reafforestation**: plant trees where forests were cut.
**Afforestation**: plant trees where there were none.

cards.title: How trees help
body: Rain hits the ground more gently under trees.
Roots hold soil. Water soaks down.

cards.title: Control: dams
body: Build **dams** on the **upper course** of rivers.
They hold extra water and trap soil.

cards.title: Control: farming
body: **Contour ploughing** across the slope lets water soak in.
**Terracing** makes steps that hold the water.

cards.title: Ways to stop floods
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: Ask for help
body: The **Ministry of Agriculture** can tell you which trees to plant.

cards.q: Why do towns flood more easily?

options.B: Tar and cement stop rain soaking in

cards.why: Tarred and cemented surfaces cannot absorb rain water.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Floods: heavy rain, deforestation, towns.
Stop them: trees, dams, contour ploughing, terracing.

cards.title: What is drought?
body: A **drought** is a long dry time with **little or no rain**.

cards.title: Where?
body: Droughts are common in the **Sahel**: Eritrea, northern Sudan, Chad, Niger and Mali.

cards.title: Effects
body: The land gets very dry. Wind blows the soil away.
**Crops fail** and animals die. This leads to **famine**.

cards.title: Most common
body: Drought is the **most common** disaster in many parts of Africa.

cards.title: Trees and rain
body: Move the slider.

states.label: With trees
states.text: Trees give off water (**transpiration**). It makes clouds and rain.

states.label: No trees
states.text: With no plants there is less water vapour, so less rain. **Drought** follows.

cards.title: Cause: clearing land
body: Cutting forests for farms removes the **vegetation cover**.

cards.title: Cause: overgrazing
body: Too many animals eat all the grass, even the roots.
The soil becomes **bare**.

cards.title: How to cope with drought
head: Do this
Why
rows: Grow food crops, not cash crops

cards.title: Cash crops
body: **Cash crops** are grown to **sell**.
In Eritrea, coffee and cotton are cash crops.

cards.q: Which crops are safer in dry soil?
cards.why: Sorghum and millet are drought-resistant.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Drought: long dry time. Causes: cutting trees, overgrazing.
Cope: trees, dams, cisterns, fewer animals, store food.

cards.title: What is lightning?
body: **Lightning** is a flash of **electricity**.
It goes from cloud to cloud, or from cloud to ground.

cards.title: Danger
body: Lightning can kill people and animals.
If it hits trees it can start a **bush fire**.

cards.title: Stay safe
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: Lightning safety
head: Rule
rows: Do not plant trees close to houses.
Cut branches of trees near houses.
Do not use the telephone during lightning.

cards.q: During lightning you should NOT:
cards.why: The book says do not use the telephone during lightning.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Lightning = electricity. No phone, no trees near houses.

a disaster caused by nature
when a river overflows its banks
a long dry time with little or no rain
a flash of electricity from the clouds
when people have no food
planting trees where forests were cut
more people living in towns and cities
water leaving plants through their leaves
soaked; full of water
a tank that collects rain from roofs

a black sticky material for roads

tips.text: Flood = too much water. Drought = too little.
Trees help with both floods and droughts.
Lightning: no phone, no trees by the house.

items.text: Drought is the most common disaster in many parts of Africa.
Coffee is a drought-resistant food crop.
items.why: Coffee is a cash crop; sorghum and millet resist drought.

items.text: Water tanks for roof rain are called ___.
Crops grown to sell are ___ crops.
Build dams on the ___ course of rivers.

cards.back: Planting trees where there were none.

questions.q: What is a flood?
questions.answer: When a river has too much water and overflows its banks.
why: Flooding happens when the river channel cannot contain the water.

similar.a: Heavy rain for hours or days.

questions.q: What is drought?
questions.answer: A long dry period with little or no rain.
why: Drought is a long, dry period with little or no rainfall.

similar.a: The Sahel: Eritrea, Sudan, Chad, Niger, Mali.

questions.q: What is lightning?
questions.answer: A flash of electricity from cloud to cloud or cloud to ground.
why: Lightning is a flash of electricity.

questions.q: What is reafforestation?
questions.answer: Planting trees in areas where forests were cut down.
why: Reafforestation is planting trees in deforested areas.

similar.a: Planting trees where there was no forest.

questions.q: How does deforestation cause floods?

options.B: Soil washes into rivers and makes them shallow

why: Eroded soil fills river beds, so rivers overflow.

similar.q: What else causes floods in towns?
similar.a: Tar and cement stop rain soaking in.

questions.q: Where should dams be built to control floods?
why: Dams at the upper course hold extra water.

questions.q: Overgrazing can lead to drought.
why: Overgrazing leaves bare soil, no transpiration, and less rain.

questions.q: Coffee and cotton are grown in Eritrea as ___ crops.
why: Cash crops are grown mainly for sale.

similar.q: What should farmers grow in drought?

questions.q: How can we protect ourselves from lightning?
why: Do not use the telephone; keep trees away from houses; cut near branches.

questions.q: Give two ways to cope with drought.
questions.answer: Plant trees, build dams or ponds, build cisterns, keep fewer animals, store food, grow sorghum and millet.
why: The book lists eight ways, including trees, dams, cisterns and storing food.

questions.q: Saturated ground can absorb a lot more rain water.
why: Saturated (soaked) ground cannot absorb any more water.

similar.q: What happens to the extra water?
similar.a: It flows over the surface and floods.

questions.q: Neem is an example of a:
why: The book names neem as a fast-growing tree.

similar.q: Name another type of tree to plant.

units.title: Caring for Younger Children
units.intro: In this unit you learn about kinds of families, being companions to younger brothers and sisters, and keeping small children safe at home.

pins.text: Dog: the child pulls its tail
Medicine bottle and scissors on a table

cards.title: Three kinds of family
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Extended
states.text: **Extended family**: grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and children.

states.label: Nuclear
states.text: **Nuclear family**: mother, father and children only.

states.label: Single parent
states.text: **Single parent family**: one parent and the children.

cards.title: Step-families
body: Some families have **step-parents**.
Some have **half brothers** and **half sisters**.

cards.title: Helping each other
body: Family members live together.
They **depend on each other** every day.

steps.text: **Amal** is in grade six. Her father is **Mr. Jemal**.
Her mother died when Amal was **two**.
Her father married **Mrs. Meriem**. She is Amal's **step-mother**.
A year later **Abdu** was born. He is Amal's **half-brother**.
Amal helps look after Abdu and makes tea for her father. She is **happy**.

cards.title: Older brothers and sisters
body: Young children spend a lot of time with older brothers and sisters.
They **admire** and **copy** them.

cards.q: Mother, father and children only is a:
cards.why: A nuclear family has only a mother, a father and children.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Extended = many relatives. Nuclear = parents + children. Single parent = one parent.

cards.title: Companions
body: A **companion** is someone you spend a lot of time with.

cards.title: Always with you
body: Younger brothers and sisters try to **help** you.
They **cooperate** and **share** things with you.

cards.title: Things we do together
head: Activity
rows: Sharing pencils, a ruler, a football

cards.title: Make a bar graph
body: The book asks each pupil to choose **three** important activities.
Then show the choices in a **bar graph**.

cards.q: To cooperate means to:
cards.why: Cooperate means to work or act together with others.

cards.title: Fraternal love
body: Older children love their younger brothers and sisters.
They give **advice** and show **good behaviour**.

cards.title: A new baby
body: When a new baby comes, don't feel **jealous**.
You are not losing anything. You are **gaining a new friend**.

cards.q: When a new baby is born, an older child should:
cards.why: The older child gains a new friend in the family.

cards.title: Babies move around
body: Babies that move around the house can meet **dangers**.

cards.title: Spot the dangers
body: The book's pictures show these dangers. Tap each dot.

cards.title: Amal and the stove
body: Amal put a kettle on the stove to make tea for her friend Zaid.
Abdu went near and **touched the kettle**.

cards.title: Amal acts fast
body: Amal **pulled Abdu away** from the stove.
She checked his hands. There were **no burns**.

cards.title: Thank you, Amal
body: Amal told Meriem what happened.
Meriem **thanked** her for looking after Abdu.

cards.title: Keep them safe
body: Very young children can get into **danger**.
Older children should keep them **safe and healthy**.

cards.title: Feeling secure
body: Younger children feel **secure** with older children.

cards.q: What did Amal do when Abdu touched the kettle?

options.B: Pulled him away from the stove

cards.why: She rushed and pulled him away, then checked his hands.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Watch young children near stoves, sockets, stairs, dogs and medicine.
Older children keep younger ones safe.

glossary.meaning: a group of one or two parents and their children
mother, father and children only
a family with uncles, aunts, cousins and grandparents who help each other
one parent and the children
a woman married to your father who is not your birth mother
a brother who shares only one parent with you
a grown-up person

to work together with others
a part of something divided between people
the way a person acts
an unexpected event that causes damage or injury
unhappy because someone else gets attention

tips.text: Nuclear = the core: mum, dad, kids.
New baby = new friend, not a rival.
Babies + stove = danger. Stay close!

items.text: If a new baby is born you should feel jealous.
Family members depend on each other every day.
Only sisters should help parents with housework.
items.why: Brothers and sisters can all help.

items.text: Younger children often copy older brothers and sisters.

cards.back: Someone you spend much time with.

questions.q: Write three things at home that can be dangerous for a baby.
questions.answer: E.g. electric sockets, a hot stove, stairs, medicine, a dog.
why: The book's pictures show a socket, a stove, a dog, a table with medicine, and stairs.

similar.a: A hot kettle on the stove.

questions.q: If a new baby is born in your family you should feel jealous.
why: The older child is not losing anything; they gain a new friend.

similar.q: What do older children give younger ones?

questions.q: Family members depend upon each other in their daily activities.
why: The book says they live together and depend on each other.

similar.q: Name the three kinds of family.

questions.q: Only sisters should help parents in doing household work.
why: All children can help their families.

similar.a: She looks after Abdu and makes tea.

questions.q: A family with grandparents, uncles and aunts is:
why: The extended family includes grandparents, uncles and aunts.

questions.q: Who is Abdu to Amal?
why: Abdu is the son of Amal's father and step-mother.

questions.q: Teasing friends is ___ behaviour.
why: Teasing friends is bad behaviour.

similar.q: Is respecting elders good or bad?

questions.q: How did Amal prevent a serious accident?
questions.answer: She pulled Abdu away from the burning stove and checked his hands.
why: She rushed to Abdu and pulled him away from the stove.

questions.q: Younger children often:
why: They admire older brothers and sisters and copy them.

similar.a: Someone you spend much time with.

questions.q: To work or act together with others is to ___.
why: Cooperate means to work or act together with others.

similar.a: An unexpected event that causes injury.

questions.q: Younger children feel secure with older children.
why: The summary says younger children feel secure with older children.
